a:r.a:t: (suffix, Latin): to love, or demonstrate fondess towards
Nucleophiles love nuclei. The nuclei of an atom contains positively charged particles (protons), so nucleophiles love to react with positive charges and are electron rich.
Electrophiles love electrons. Electrons are negatively charged, so electrophiles must be positively charged.

p:cNvPr.descr: Structures and descriptions of common nucleophiles and electrophiles. The figure is split into 2 columns: nucleophiles and electrophiles, both labeled above. The nucleophile column, on the left, begins with a negatively charged oxygen. It is an O with a left bond, two red electrons on its right side, and a negative sign. From the negative sign there is a downward curved right arrow. Red dots represent electrons; red arrows represent electron transfer. Below, there is text reading: "Negatively charged oxygen (as in an unprotonated hydroxyl group or an ionized carboxylic acid)." Below this, there is an S with a left bond, 2 electrons on its right, a negative sign, and a downward curved red arrow. Below that, there is a label reading, "Negatively charged sulfhydryl." Below this there is a C with 3 bonds at the left, top, and bottom, with 2 electrons on the right and a negative sign, with a downward curved red arrow. It is labeled "carbanion." Below this is an N with 3 bonds, left, right, and down, and two electrons on top with a curved downward red arrow. It is labeled "uncharged amine group" below. Below this is a 5-sided ring, with an NH bonded up and right to C, which double bonds right to C, down and right to N, with double bonds down and left to C, which bonds up and left to NH. The N on the right has 2 electrons shown with a downward curved red arrow. It is labeled "imidazole" below. At the bottom there is an O bonded left to an H. The O has 2 red electrons and a negative sign above, with a curved red arrow from the negative sign. It is labeled "hydroxide ion." The column on the right shows common electrophiles. Below the title is the first structure, which consists of a C with 2 bonds, right and left, and a downward double bond to O. Above, there is an R group with 2 electrons and a downward red arrow transferring electrons to the C. Another electron transfer takes place to the double-bonded O. Below, there is text that reads, "Carbon atom of a carbonyl group (the more electronegative oxygen of the carbonyl group pulls electrons away from the carbon)." Below this is another structure, a C with 2 bonds, upper left and lower left, double bonded right to N+, which has a right bond and a bond down to H. Above is an R with 2 electrons, transferring electrons to the C, which then gets transferred down from the double bond to the N. Below, there is text reading, "Protonated imine group (activated for nucleophilic attack at the carbon by protonation of the imine)." Below this is a P bonded up, left, and down to O minus, and double bonded right to O. To the upper right is an R with 2 electrons, transferring electrons to the P, which then get transferred from the double bond to the O. Below, there is text that reads, "Phosphorus of a phosphate group." Below this, the final diagram shows an H+ with an R with 2 electrons transferring electrons down to the H+. It is labeled below "proton."
